definitions.definition: The self: in the Upaniṣads the innermost reality of a person — the seer of seeing that cannot be seen (BAU 3.4.2), the inner controller (BAU 3.7), the light of a person (BAU 4.3.6) — which is declared to be brahman (BAU 1.4.10, 2.5.19; ChU 6.8.7; MāU 2). The word also means body or oneself in narrative passages (ChU 8.8.4).

cross_language.note: the Buddhist texts deny a permanent attā; same word, opposed doctrine

definitions.definition: The ultimate ground: that from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they go (TU 3.1.1); being, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1); truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1); understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); described also by negation (BAU 2.3.6). Also the name of the formula or sacred word in older usage.

cross_language.note: used in Pali mostly for the deity Brahmā or as 'excellent'

definitions.definition: The person: the self-born person at creation (BAU 1.4.1; AU 1.1.3); the inner person in the eye or heart; in KU 1.3.11 the highest principle beyond the unmanifest; in MuU 2.1.2 the divine formless person; in ŚU 3.8-15 the great person of the Puruṣa Sūkta.

The living self: the 'living self' (jīva ātman) with which being enters the elements (ChU 6.3.2); life which does not die when the body dies (ChU 6.11.3); in ŚU 5.9 the jīva is a hundredth part of a hundredth of a hair's tip yet fit for infinity.

literal: the one who controls from within

definitions.definition: The inner controller: 'he who dwells in the earth yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who controls it from within' — the self, the immortal (BAU 3.7).

The imperishable: that on which space is woven, described by negations (BAU 3.8.8), by whose command sun and moon stand apart (3.8.9); the object of the higher knowledge (MuU 1.1.5); also 'syllable', especially Om (ChU 1.1.1; KU 1.2.16; MāU 1).
The perishable, paired with the imperishable: primal matter (pradhāna) is the perishable, Hara the imperishable (ŚU 1.10); the perishable is ignorance (ŚU 5.1).
Plenitude: that in which one sees, hears and understands nothing else; it is happiness and immortal, established in its own greatness (ChU 7.23-24).

Full, complete: 'that is full, this is full; from the full the full arises; taking the full from the full, the full remains' (BAU 5.1.1); the space within the heart is full and unchanging (ChU 3.12.9).
Being: 'in the beginning this was being alone, one without a second' (ChU 6.2.1); in BAU 2.3.1 and TU 2.6 paired with tyat/tyam as the manifest and the beyond.
Non-being: some said this was non-being in the beginning (rejected in ChU 6.2.1-2); TU 2.7 and ChU 3.19.1 say non-being was first and being came from it.

The real, truth: 'the real behind the real' is the hidden name of the self (BAU 2.1.20, 2.3.6); analysed as sa-ti-yam (BAU 5.5.1; ChU 8.3.5); truth-speaking as a virtue (TU 1.11; MuU 3.1.6) and as protection in the axe ordeal (ChU 6.16).
What is right, the order: spoken alongside truth (TU 1.1, 1.9); the right side of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the knower is 'first-born of ṛta' (TU 3.10.6).

Bliss: brahman is bliss (TU 3.6); the self made of bliss (TU 2.5); brahman is understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); the highest bliss of the brahma-world on a fraction of which others live (BAU 4.3.32); measured in the calculus of bliss (TU 2.8; BAU 4.3.33).
Intelligence, cognition: the sixteen faculties of heart and mind are its names; 'the world is guided by intelligence; intelligence is brahman' (AU 3.1.2-3).

Wisdom, intelligence: the wise brahmin should cultivate prajñā (BAU 4.4.21); Indra as 'breath, the intelligent self' (prajñātman, KauU 3.2); by intelligence one obtains thoughts and desires (KauU 1.7).
The 'intelligent one', the third quarter of the self, whose field is deep sleep, a mass of cognition, made of bliss (MāU 5); the intelligent self that embraces the sleeper (BAU 4.3.21).
Understanding: a rung in Sanatkumāra's ladder (ChU 7.7, 7.17); the self made of understanding (TU 2.4; BAU 4.3.7); brahman is understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28).

cross_language.note: Buddhist sense: consciousness as an aggregate

definitions.definition: A solid mass of cognition: the great being is a mass of understanding like salt dissolved in water (BAU 2.4.12, 4.5.13); the sleeper as prājña is a mass of cognition (MāU 5).
Self-luminous: in dream 'here the person becomes his own light' (BAU 4.3.9, 4.3.14); the self is the light of a person when sun, moon, fire and speech are gone (4.3.6).
Light: the light beyond heaven which is the light within a person (ChU 3.13.7); the highest light which the serene one reaches (ChU 8.3.4, 8.12.3); the light of lights (MuU 2.2.9).
The serene one: the self that, rising from the body and reaching the highest light, appears in its own form (ChU 8.3.4, 8.12.3); also the state of deep serenity (BAU 4.3.15).
Fearlessness: 'brahman is fearlessness' (BAU 4.4.25); Janaka has reached fearlessness (4.2.4); fear arises from a second (1.4.2); the knower of bliss is never afraid (TU 2.4, 2.9).
Without a second, non-dual: 'he becomes the ocean, the one seer without duality' (BAU 4.3.32); the fourth is 'peaceful, auspicious, non-dual' (MāU 7, 12).

notes: The adjective of the Upaniṣads; the school-name Advaita Vedānta is later.

definitions.definition: Duality: 'where there is duality, as it were, one sees another' (BAU 2.4.14, 4.5.15).

'Not so, not so': the instruction (ādeśa) about brahman/the self, for there is nothing beyond this 'not so' (BAU 2.3.6); the self is 'not this, not this' — ungraspable, indestructible, unattached (BAU 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15). In BAU 3.2.11 and 4.5.3 the same words are an ordinary double negative.
Instruction, teaching formula: 'now the instruction: not so, not so' (BAU 2.3.6); the teaching about brahman in lightning and in the mind (Kena 4.4-5); the teaching of 'I' and of the self (ChU 7.25).

'Great saying': a later (Advaita) name for four Upaniṣadic statements of identity, one from each Veda — prajñānaṃ brahma (AU 3.1.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (BAU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (ChU 6.8.7), ayam ātmā brahma (MāU 2; BAU 2.5.19). The word does not occur in these texts.
The fourth: beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; neither inward- nor outward-knowing, the stilling of the world, non-dual (MāU 7, 12, where the word is caturtha); turya in MaiU 6.19 and 7.11.
Waking: the field of the first quarter, vaiśvānara, outward-knowing, enjoying the gross (MāU 3).

Dream: the junction between this world and the other, where the person is his own light and creates chariots and roads (BAU 4.3.9-10); the field of taijasa (MāU 4); where the mind experiences its greatness (PrU 4.5).
Deep sleep: where one desires no desire and sees no dream (BAU 4.3.19; MāU 5); one has merged with being (ChU 6.8.1); one lies in the hitā channels (BAU 2.1.19).
'Common to all men': the self conceived as the cosmos with sky as head etc. (ChU 5.11-18); the first quarter, waking (MāU 3); the digestive fire within a person (BAU 5.9.1).
'The brilliant one': the second quarter of the self, whose field is dream (MāU 4).

Breath, life-breath: the eldest and best of the vital powers (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1); the one god (BAU 3.9.9); the gatherer in the body (ChU 4.3.3); born from the self like a shadow (PrU 3.3); brahman (KauU 2.1) and 'the intelligent self' (KauU 3.2); also the collective name of the five breaths (BAU 1.5.3).
The downward (or out-) breath; in PrU 3.5 it is in the organs of excretion and generation; the navel's function whose deity is death (AU 1.1.4).
The diffused breath, moving through the channels (PrU 3.6); the right side of the self made of breath (TU 2.2).
The up-breath, which through one channel leads upward at death — to a world of merit, of evil or of humans (PrU 3.7); identified with heat (PrU 3.9).
The equalizing breath in the middle of the body, distributing food (PrU 3.5).

The heart: seat of the self and of the space within it (ChU 3.14.3, 8.1.1-3); analysed as 'hṛdi ayam', 'this is in the heart' (ChU 8.3.3) and as hṛ-da-yam (BAU 5.3.1); where the knots and desires dwell (KU 2.3.14-15).
The small (space): 'in this city of brahman is a small lotus-dwelling, within it a small space; what is within that is to be sought' (ChU 8.1.1).

equivalents.note: the dahara is the space within the heart, not the heart itself

definitions.definition: The cave: the hidden place (in the heart) where the self or brahman is set (TU 2.1.1; KU 1.2.12, 1.2.20, 1.3.1; MuU 2.1.10).
Channel: 101 channels of the heart, one leading to the crown (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); 72,000 branch channels (PrU 3.6); the suṣumnā (MaiU 6.21).
The channels called hitā, extending from the heart, fine as a hair split a thousandfold, into which the self slips in deep sleep (BAU 2.1.19, 4.3.20; KauU 4.19).
The upward channel carrying breath, divided within the palate, through which, joined with breath, Om and mind, one goes upward (MaiU 6.21) — the earliest use of the name in these texts.
The cleft: the suture at the top of the skull through which the self entered the body (AU 1.3.12).

notes: Later traditions speak of the brahmarandhra.

definitions.definition: 'Indra's birthplace': the passage between the palates, where the hair parts, by which the person made of mind goes out (TU 1.6.1).
The person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body or the heart, lord of past and future (KU 2.1.12-13, 2.3.17; ŚU 3.13, 5.8).
Minute, 'smaller than the small': the self in the heart smaller than a grain yet greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3; KU 1.2.20; ŚU 3.20).
Sheath, case: the golden sheath in which brahman is (MuU 2.2.9); the cosmic chest (ChU 3.15). The later Vedānta name 'pañca-kośa' for the five selves of TU 2 is not used in the TU itself.
Made of (the essence of) food: the outermost self, the person formed from food (TU 2.1).
Made of breath: the self within the food-self, with prāṇa as head (TU 2.2).
Made of mind: the self within the breath-self (TU 2.3); also the person made of mind in the heart (TU 1.6; BAU 5.6; ChU 3.14.2).
Made of understanding: the self within the mind-self, with faith as head and yoga as trunk (TU 2.4); the person made of understanding among the breaths (BAU 4.3.7).
Made of bliss: the innermost of the five selves, whose tail and foundation is brahman (TU 2.5).

The person of sixteen parts (kalā): shown by fasting to depend on food (ChU 6.7); in PrU 6 the parts arising from breath (faith, space, wind, light, water, earth, senses, mind, food, strength, austerity, mantras, rites, worlds, name) which vanish into the person as rivers into the ocean.
Matter (wealth, substance): paired with breath as the first pair produced by Prajāpati; the moon, and all that has form or is formless (PrU 1.4-5); the southern course (1.9).

Heat, radiance: the first emanation of being, which produced water (ChU 6.2.3); its finest part is speech (6.5.4); in dying breath goes into heat (6.8.6); in deep sleep the mind is overcome by tejas (PrU 4.6).
Food: brahman is food (TU 3.2); the person is made of the essence of food (TU 2.1); vows about food (TU 3.7-10); mind is made of food (ChU 6.5.4, 6.7); 'I am food' sings the knower (TU 3.10.6).

Space: the final support from which all beings arise and into which they return (ChU 1.9.1); the accomplisher of name and form (ChU 8.14.1); the first element to arise from the self (TU 2.1); the space within the heart (ChU 8.1.3); 'kha' is brahman (ChU 4.10.4; BAU 5.1.1).
Speech: one of the vital functions contending with breath (BAU 1.3; ChU 5.1); fire becoming speech entered the mouth (AU 1.2.4); in the inner agnihotra speech is offered into breath (KauU 2.5).

Mind: made of food (ChU 6.5.4); desire, intention, doubt, faith, shame, fear are all mind (BAU 1.5.3); the reins of the chariot (KU 1.3.3); 'the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation' (MaiU 6.34); 'by the mind alone is it to be seen' (BAU 4.4.19).
Intellect: the charioteer (KU 1.3.3); higher than mind, below the great self (KU 1.3.10); it does not stir in the highest state (KU 2.3.10).

Thought: a rung above intention in Sanatkumāra's ladder (ChU 7.5); with whatever thought one has one enters breath at death (PrU 3.10); 'the mind alone is saṃsāra' (cittam eva hi saṃsāraḥ, MaiU 6.34).

The I-maker: the 'teaching of I' (ahaṃkārādeśa) precedes the teaching of the self (ChU 7.25.1); listed among the faculties resting in the self (PrU 4.8); the jīva is endowed with intention and ahaṃkāra (ŚU 5.8).

Intention: a rung of the ladder (ChU 7.4); the self's intentions are real (ChU 8.1.5, 8.7.1); by intention alone the fathers' world arises (8.2.1); 'intention' is the teaching about brahman with respect to the self (Kena 4.5).
Resolve, will: 'a person is made of resolve; as his resolve here, so he becomes on departing' (ChU 3.14.1; cf. BAU 4.4.5); 'O resolve (mind), remember' (Īśa 17).

Desire: 'a person is made of desire' (BAU 4.4.5); the desiring one returns for action, the one without desire goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.6); when all desires in the heart are released the mortal becomes immortal (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14). The self's 'real desires' (ChU 8.1.5) are distinguished from ordinary ones.

Action and its result: 'one becomes good by good action, bad by bad action' (BAU 3.2.13); 'as one acts, so one becomes' (BAU 4.4.5); rebirth 'according to action and learning' (KU 2.2.7; KauU 1.2); action does not cling to one who knows (ChU 4.14.3; Īśa 2).

cross_language.note: same word; doctrines differ in detail

definitions.definition: The round (of rebirth): the one without understanding goes on in saṃsāra (KU 1.3.7); God is the cause of saṃsāra and liberation (ŚU 6.16); 'the mind alone is saṃsāra' (MaiU 6.34).

Release: rare as a noun in the early prose Upaniṣads, which speak of immortality (amṛtatva); 'freed, he is freed' (KU 2.2.1); release (vimokṣa) for one who has a teacher (ChU 6.14.2); the cause of saṃsāra and mokṣa (ŚU 6.16); 'the mark of liberation' (MaiU 6.20); 'desiring liberation (mumukṣu) I go for refuge' (ŚU 6.18).

Immortality: the goal named by the early Upaniṣads — 'there is no hope of immortality through wealth' (BAU 2.4.2); 'so much is immortality' (4.5.15); 'the mortal becomes immortal' (4.4.7; KU 2.3.14); 'lead me from death to immortality' (BAU 1.3.28).

equivalents.note: the early texts' 'immortality' is what the later texts (ŚU 6.16, MaiU 6.20) call mokṣa; the early texts do not themselves equate the two words

definitions.definition: The path of the gods: through flame, day, the waxing fortnight, the northern course, the year (or the gods' world), the sun, the moon and lightning, where a non-human person leads to brahman; those who go by it do not return (ChU 4.15.5, 5.10.1-2; BAU 6.2.15; PrU 1.10; KauU 1.3).

The path of the fathers: through smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern course, the fathers' world, space and the moon, and back as rain and food into a womb (ChU 5.10.3-6; BAU 6.2.16; PrU 1.9).

The knowledge of the five fires: yonder world, the rain-god, the earth, man and woman as sacrificial fires, into which faith, Soma, rain, food and semen are offered, so that the waters come to be called person at the fifth offering (ChU 5.3-10; BAU 6.2).
Sacrifices and works of merit (such as digging wells): those who venerate them win the moon and return (ChU 5.10.3; PrU 1.9); fools who think them best go to lower worlds (MuU 1.2.10).

The world of brahman: reached by the path of the gods (BAU 6.2.15) and by brahmacarya (ChU 8.4-5); described with its lake, river, tree, city and palace (KauU 1.3-5; ChU 8.5.3); in BAU 4.3.32 the ocean-like non-dual seer 'is the world of brahman'.

Knowledge: what is done with knowledge is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10); the world of the gods is won by knowledge (BAU 1.5.16); paired with avidyā (Īśa 9-11; KU 1.2.4; ŚU 5.1); the higher and lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.4).

Ignorance: those living in it think themselves wise and go round like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 pairs it with vidyā (read by some as rites); the perishable is avidyā (ŚU 5.1); the teacher takes one across to the far shore of avidyā (PrU 6.8).
The higher knowledge: that by which the imperishable is grasped (MuU 1.1.5).
The lower knowledge: the four Vedas and the six ancillary sciences (MuU 1.1.5).
Knowledge of brahman, 'the foundation of all knowledge', taught by Brahmā to Atharvan (MuU 1.1.1); to be taught only to those who performed the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10).

Secret teaching, hidden connection or name: 'its upaniṣad is the real behind the real' (BAU 2.1.20); the upaniṣad of the asuras (ChU 8.8.4); 'we have told you the upaniṣad about brahman' (Kena 4.7); what is done with the upaniṣad is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10).
Veneration, meditation: venerating X as brahman (ChU 7; BAU 4.1); 'one should venerate it as the self' (BAU 1.4.7); 'not this that people venerate here' (Kena 1.5).

The syllable Om: the udgītha (ChU 1.1.1); brahman and all this (TU 1.8; MāU 1); the word all Vedas proclaim (KU 1.2.15); the bow (MuU 2.2.4); the higher and lower brahman (PrU 5.2); its measures A, U, M and the measureless (MāU 8-12).
Om as the sacred syllable: 'praṇava is the bow' (MuU 2.2.4); the upper fire-stick of meditation (ŚU 1.14).
The loud chant of the Sāman singer, venerated as Om and as breath (ChU 1.1-1.12; BAU 1.3).
The calls bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ (and mahaḥ): meditated on as worlds, lights, Vedas and breaths (TU 1.5); flowed from the Veda at creation (ChU 2.23.2).
Word-brahman: of the two brahmans, sound and non-sound, one skilled in the word-brahman attains the highest (MaiU 6.22).
The stilling of the world's diversity: an epithet of the fourth (MāU 7, 12).

notes: The same compound appears in the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (src:mulamadhyamakakarika); see brw:mandukya-madhyamaka-prapancopasama.

definitions.definition: Yoga: 'the firm holding of the senses' (KU 2.3.11); the method taught by Death (KU 2.3.18); the trunk of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the chapter on posture, breath and signs (ŚU 2); the six-limbed yoga (MaiU 6.18).
The yoga of the inner self, by which the wise one realizes the hidden god and leaves joy and sorrow (KU 1.2.12).
The six-limbed yoga of the Maitrī: breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, concentration, contemplative reasoning and absorption (MaiU 6.18).

notes: The Kālacakra six-branch yoga has the same name and a different list (other units).

definitions.definition: Breath-control: first limb of the Maitrī's yoga (MaiU 6.18); ŚU 2.9 describes restraining the breaths and breathing out gently through the nose.
Withdrawal (of the senses): second limb of the Maitrī's yoga (MaiU 6.18); cf. drawing the senses into the heart (ŚU 2.8) and turning the sight inward (KU 2.1.1).

Meditation: a rung of the ladder (ChU 7.6); the 'yoga of meditation' by which the sages saw God's power (ŚU 1.3); the friction of meditation (ŚU 1.14); a limb in MaiU 6.18; one sees him 'meditating' (MuU 3.1.8).
Holding, concentration: yoga is the firm holding (dhāraṇā) of the senses (KU 2.3.11); fourth limb in MaiU 6.18.
Reasoning: 'this understanding is not to be gained by reasoning' (KU 1.2.9); yet in MaiU 6.18 and 6.20 tarka is a limb of yoga, contemplative reasoning by which brahman is seen.

Absorption, collectedness: the one 'not collected' cannot attain it (KU 1.2.24, asamāhita); 'samāhita' among the virtues of BAU 4.4.23; the sixth limb (MaiU 6.18); the happiness of a mind washed by samādhi (MaiU 6.34).
Self-restraint: the gods' 'da' (BAU 5.2); among the virtues of BAU 4.4.23 (dānta); foundation of the upaniṣad with austerity and work (Kena 4.8).
Giving: the humans' 'da' (BAU 5.2); 'give with faith' (TU 1.11.3); a priestly gift of the life-sacrifice (ChU 3.17.4).
Compassion: the asuras' 'da' — be compassionate (dayadhvam) (BAU 5.2.3).

Austerity, heat: by tapas Prajāpati and brahman create (TU 2.6; PrU 1.4; MuU 1.1.8); Bhṛgu seeks brahman by tapas — 'tapas is brahman' (TU 3.2); a branch of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); sickness and cremation as the supreme tapas (BAU 5.11).
Faith: offered by the gods into the fire of yonder world (ChU 5.4; BAU 6.2.9); 'have faith' (ChU 6.12.2); head of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); 'give with faith' (TU 1.11).
Recitation (study) of one's Veda: 'do not neglect study' (TU 1.11); all duties 'with study and teaching' (TU 1.9); the householder keeps reciting (ChU 8.15).

The life of a student of the Veda, celibacy: what people call sacrifice is really brahmacarya (ChU 8.5); the brahma-world belongs to those who find it by brahmacarya (ChU 8.4.3); preparatory year of austerity, celibacy and faith (PrU 1.2).
Vow, observance: the vow of breathing (BAU 1.5.23); the food vows (TU 3.7-10); the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10); Prajāpati's vow (PrU 1.13).
The 'vow of the head', which qualifies one to receive the knowledge of brahman (MuU 3.2.10); its nature is not explained in the text (commentators differ).
Purity of food (or of what is taken in): from it purity of mind, firm memory and the loosening of all knots (ChU 7.26.2).
'With fuel in hand': the way a pupil approaches a teacher (MuU 1.2.12; PrU 1.1; ChU 5.11.7, 8.7.2; KauU 1.1).
Teacher: 'he should go to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in brahman' (MuU 1.2.12); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).
Teacher: knowledge learned from a teacher leads most surely to the goal (ChU 4.9.3); 'a person who has a teacher knows' (ChU 6.14.2); 'let your teacher be a god to you' (TU 1.11.2).
The wise, steadfast one: chooses the good over the pleasant (KU 1.2.2); turns his sight inward (KU 2.1.1).
The good, the better: chosen by the wise over the pleasant (KU 1.2.1-2).
The pleasant: chosen by the fool for the sake of getting and keeping (KU 1.2.2).
Desire, pursuit: the three desires — for sons, for wealth and for worlds — which knowers of the self rise above to live as mendicants (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22).
Living on alms, the mendicant's life (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22; cf. MuU 1.2.11).
Silent sage: 'having done with learning and childhood he becomes a muni' (BAU 3.5.1); 'knowing it one becomes a muni' (BAU 4.4.22).

Renunciation: ascetics purified by 'the yoga of renunciation' (saṃnyāsa-yoga) are released in the brahma-worlds (MuU 3.2.6), an early occurrence of the word; the practice itself is described in BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22.
Ascetic, striver: the yatis who have ascertained the meaning of Vedānta (MuU 3.2.6).

Stage of life: 'proceeding through one's own āśramas' is part of the remedy (MaiU 4.3); ŚU 6.21 names those beyond the āśramas (atyāśramin); ChU 2.23.1 has three 'branches of dharma' without the word.
One beyond the stages of life, to whom Śvetāśvatara declared brahman (ŚU 6.21).

Dharma: created by brahman as the power of the ruling power, higher than all; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); Naciketas asks for what is other than dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14); one's own dharma rescues the elemental self (MaiU 4.3).
The inner fire-offering of Pratardana: offering breath into speech while speaking and speech into breath while breathing, continually, waking or asleep (KauU 2.5).

The fire-offering into the breaths: in ChU 5.19-24 the first morsels of food are offered to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna as an agnihotra into the vaiśvānara self; the name is from later texts (e.g., the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad).
The transfer from a dying father to his son (BAU 1.5.17; KauU 2.15).
The Nāciketa fire, the fire-altar leading to heaven taught by Yama as the second boon; one who piles it three times crosses birth and death (KU 1.1.14-18).

Serenity; grace: 'through the serenity of the constituents' (dhātuprasāda, KU 1.2.20) or 'through the grace of the creator' (dhātuḥ prasāda, ŚU 3.20); by the serenity of knowledge one sees the partless (MuU 3.1.8); by God's grace Śvetāśvatara knew brahman (ŚU 6.21); by serenity of mind one destroys karma (MaiU 6.20, 6.34).
Devotion: 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23).
Going for refuge: 'I, desiring liberation, go for refuge (śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye) to that God' (ŚU 6.18); the verb, not the later noun, is used.

The Lord: all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord (Īśa 1); the two birds, the Lord and the one who grieves (MuU 3.1.2); the great Lord of lords (ŚU 6.7); the māyin (ŚU 4.10); lord of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6).
Rudra: 'Rudra is one, they do not stand for a second' (ŚU 3.2); source of the gods, who saw Hiraṇyagarbha born (3.4); his auspicious form (3.5); in MaiU 5.2 the tamas-part of the one.
Auspicious; Śiva: 'therefore he is Śiva, present everywhere' (ŚU 3.11); 'knowing Śiva hidden in all beings' (4.14-16); 'Śiva alone' (4.18); the fourth is śiva, auspicious (MāU 7).

Power, magic, illusion; deceit: Indra goes about in many forms by his māyās (BAU 2.5.19); know prakṛti to be māyā and the great Lord the māyin (ŚU 4.10); the cessation of all māyā (ŚU 1.10); in PrU 1.16 māyā is deceit.
The possessor of māyā, the great Lord who projects the world (ŚU 4.9-10).
Nature, primal matter: 'know prakṛti to be māyā' (ŚU 4.10).
Primal matter: the perishable (ŚU 1.10); God is lord of pradhāna and of the field-knower (6.16); like a spider covering himself with threads from pradhāna (6.10).
Knower of the field: God is lord of pradhāna and of the kṣetrajña (ŚU 6.16); the part that is pure consciousness in each person (MaiU 5.2).

Quality, strand: God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva is bound to the guṇas and has three guṇas (ŚU 5.7); tamas, rajas and sattva as successive states and as Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (MaiU 5.2).
The unborn (she-goat): one unborn female, red, white and black, producing many like herself, and two unborn males who enjoy and leave her (ŚU 4.5; cf. 1.9).
The wheel of brahman, in which the goose (haṃsa) wanders (ŚU 1.6) and which God's greatness turns (6.1).

Goose, swan: the self or God as the goose seated in the bright (KU 2.2.2); the goose that wanders in the wheel (ŚU 1.6); flutters outward in the city of nine gates (ŚU 3.18); the one goose in the midst of the world (6.15).
Power: the self-power of God (devātmaśakti) hidden by its qualities (ŚU 1.3); his supreme power is manifold, his innate action of knowledge and strength (6.8).
Witness: the one God is 'the witness, the knower, alone, without qualities' (ŚU 6.11).
Without qualities: said of the one God (ŚU 6.11), an early occurrence.
Alone, isolated: the knower of God is 'alone, with desires fulfilled' (ŚU 1.11); God is 'alone and without qualities' (6.11); aloneness (kevalatva) through the suṣumṇā (MaiU 6.21).
The enjoyer: the self joined with body, senses and mind (KU 1.3.4); enjoyer, enjoyed and impeller as the threefold brahman (ŚU 1.12).
The golden germ, whom Rudra saw being born (ŚU 3.4, 4.12).
The unmanifest: higher than the great self, below the person (KU 1.3.11, 2.3.8).

notes: Whether this is the Sāṃkhya pradhāna is debated (Brahma Sūtra 1.4.1).

definitions.definition: The great self: higher than the intellect, below the unmanifest (KU 1.3.10-11); speech is restrained step by step into it (KU 1.3.13).
Time: a candidate cause (ŚU 1.2) rejected as the cause (6.1); God is the maker of time (6.2, 6.16); two forms of brahman, time and the timeless (MaiU 6.15-16).
Inherent nature: a candidate cause (ŚU 1.2); those who say it is the cause are deluded (6.1).
Fixed order, necessity: listed among the candidate causes in ŚU 1.2.

notes: The same word names the Ājīvika doctrine of necessity (U33); the ŚU names no school.

definitions.definition: Chance: listed among the candidate causes in ŚU 1.2.

Name and form: the unmanifest became manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7); being entered and differentiated name and form (ChU 6.3.2); space accomplishes name and form (ChU 8.14.1); the knower is freed from name and form (MuU 3.2.8).
Making threefold: being made each of heat, water and food threefold (ChU 6.3.3-4); the later Vedānta name for the teaching (the text says 'trivṛt').
'A verbal handle': the modification is a verbal handle, a name; the reality is clay (ChU 6.1.4).
Death, as a power and as a person: death covered all at the beginning (BAU 1.2.1); death as weariness seizing the functions (BAU 1.5.21); Yama, Death, is the teacher of Naciketas (KU).
A wondrous being, the form in which brahman appears to the proud gods (Kena 3).
A name of brahman, to be venerated as 'tadvana'; all beings long for one who knows it so (Kena 4.6); the sense of the word is disputed.
Awakening: brahman 'known through each awakening' (pratibodhaviditam, Kena 2.4); the commentators interpret it variously.
With respect to the self/body, as opposed to adhidaivata, with respect to the gods: the two registers in which the Upaniṣads state correspondences (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4-5).
With respect to the gods (the cosmos), paired with adhyātma (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4).

The knot(s) of the heart: when they are cut the mortal becomes immortal (KU 2.3.15); when he is seen the knot is cut (MuU 2.2.8); the knot of ignorance (MuU 2.1.10); knots loosened by firm memory (ChU 7.26.2).
